analysis.one_liner: Limits Medicare drug copays to the drug's net-after-rebate price or its cash price, whichever is lower.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill unanimously, 45-0, but it never received a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change Medicare's prescription drug benefit so that once a senior has paid the yearly deductible but hasn't yet hit the out-of-pocket cap, their share of a drug's cost cannot be more than the drug's average net price (what the plan actually pays after manufacturer rebates) or the pharmacy's cash price, whichever is lower. Today, in that coverage phase, seniors can be charged a share of the drug's higher list price even when big rebates have already lowered what the plan really pays. It would take effect in 2027 and requires a Government Accountability Office report on how the change is working.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees who have drug costs between their deductible and the annual out-of-pocket cap. They would no longer pay cost-sharing based on a drug's inflated list price when rebates have already reduced what the plan truly pays for it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors in the Medicare drug plan coverage gap

how_it_helps.text: In the coverage phase between the deductible and the out-of-pocket threshold, a month's supply of a covered drug could cost the patient no more than the drug's average net price (what the plan pays after rebates) or the pharmacy's cash price, whichever is lower.
Low-income beneficiaries' copayments would likewise be capped at the amount allowed under the new net-price rule.
The change would apply to plan years starting on or after January 1, 2027, and the Comptroller General must report to Congress by January 1, 2029 on compliance and enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Part D insurers and the pharmacy benefit managers behind them would keep less of the gap between list prices and the lower net prices they pay after rebates. Plans could offset this by raising premiums or restricting which drugs they cover.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The rule applies only to costs between the deductible and the out-of-pocket threshold, not to a beneficiary's entire drug spending, so it does not cap all drug costs.
Plans that lose rebate revenue on covered drugs could recoup it through higher premiums or narrower formularies, shifting some of the cost back to beneficiaries in other forms.
It does not take effect until 2027 and relies on a GAO report due in 2029 to assess enforcement, so problems could persist for years before any correction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: seniors stop paying cost-sharing based on list prices that rebates have already undercut, which is money currently absorbed by plans and middlemen. The main honest objection is that insurers could shift the lost revenue into premiums or limited drug lists, and the single-phase scope leaves many drug costs untouched. On balance it is a modest, well-aimed consumer protection that quietly trimmed an insurer and middleman revenue stream.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee unanimously but was never brought up for a vote on the House floor; in December 2024 it was sent back to a subcommittee, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, joined by Rep. Brad Wenstrup, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees.
On November 15, 2023, the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee considered the bill and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.
On December 6, 2023, the full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported with amendments by a vote of 45 to 0, with no member voting against it.

After that vote, no report was filed and the bill never reached the House floor. On December 17, 2024, with the Congress weeks from ending, it was referred back to the Health Subcommittee, where it remained until the 118th Congress expired on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers came out ahead: because no vote ever occurred, they continue to keep cost-sharing tied to higher list prices rather than the lower net prices the bill would have required. Seniors keep paying the difference.

for.name: Brad Wenstrup
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its original cosponsor.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported with amendments by a 45-0 vote on December 6, 2023, after the Health Subcommittee advanced it by voice vote.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after committee approval, and on December 17, 2024 it was referred back to the Health Subcommittee, where it died when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the committee's 45-0 approval with no opposition from either party; the sponsor and cosponsor were both Republicans, and no one voted against the bill at any stage.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill would cap what beneficiaries pay at the drug's net-after-rebate price or cash price, whichever is lower, reducing the spread between list prices and actual plan costs that plans and middlemen now capture. Their interest in keeping the current arrangement runs against seniors who overpay in that coverage phase.
